name: AI glow
plain: Near-black screens with soft colored light glowing behind cards and buttons
origin: SaaS and AI landing pages, about 2020 to 2025, often traced to the Linear product site [S2]; named a 2025 web trend [S1]
defining: Brand-tinted near-black background rather than pure black, with monochrome text and high contrast [S2]
Soft halos and light blooms around buttons, navigation and key cards, sometimes pulsing on interaction [S1]
Gradient or glowing borders about 1px wide on featured cards [inferred]
Purple, blue and green gradient accents, now criticised as the default AI palette [S3][S4]
Differs from mesh-gradient: the light sits on edges and behind elements on a dark base, not as a soft full-page wash
fits: Developer tools, AI products, SaaS dashboards and launch pages
goes_wrong: Every AI product ends up looking the same, and the purple gradient reads as generic or machine-made [S3][S4]
accessibility: A glow is not a boundary: keep card and input borders at 3:1 and text at 4.5:1 on the dark base, and stop pulsing glows under reduced motion.

name: Immersive 3D web

origin: Browser WebGL showcase sites of the 2010s and 2020s; listed first among Figma's 2026 web trends [S1]
defining: Real-time 3D models people can rotate, such as a shoe spin or a virtual store tour, plus AR previews [S1]
Built with WebGL and libraries such as Three.js, often driven by scroll [S2]
Mouse-driven deformation, globe views and 3D page transitions [S3]
A full-screen canvas with sparse interface controls floating on top [inferred]
code: canvas#scene{position:fixed;inset:0;width:100vw;height:100vh;z-index:-1} /* drawn with WebGL, for example Three.js */

goes_wrong: Heavy downloads and dropped frames on mid-range phones, with content stuck behind a slow loader
accessibility: Keep text and controls in HTML rather than inside the canvas, offer a static fallback, and honour prefers-reduced-motion for camera moves.

name: Kinetic typography
plain: Words that move, stretch and change size while you watch
origin: Film title sequences of the 1950s [S4]; a web trend from 2024 to 2026 thanks to variable fonts [S1][S2]
defining: Text animates in position, scale, weight or width, often on scroll, hover or to a beat [S1][S2]
Variable fonts let weight and width shift smoothly from one font file [S2]
Stretchy, elastic letterforms that rotate or loop continuously [S5]
One short phrase per beat on a limited, high-contrast palette; square corners, radius 0 to 4px [S4]
fits: Campaign heroes, year-in-review recaps, music and event sites, social video
goes_wrong: Words never sit still long enough to read, so motion delays the message
accessibility: Hold each phrase still long enough to read, give a complete static version under prefers-reduced-motion, and never flash more than 3 times a second.

name: Type-first design
plain: Huge words fill the screen and do most of the talking
origin: Modernist print roots [S3]; named a web and brand trend for 2025 to 2026 [S1][S2]
defining: Oversized headlines set the grid and are often cropped at the screen edge [S3]
Extreme scale contrast, display text roughly 8 to 15 times body size [inferred]

fits: Brand homepages, campaigns, portfolios, museum and event identities
goes_wrong: Headlines overflow or break into single letters on phones, leaving no room for content
accessibility: Use fluid sizes that reflow at 320px wide, keep headlines as real text rather than images, and never crop away words that carry meaning.

name: Scrollytelling
plain: The story builds and changes as you scroll down
origin: Online journalism, popularised by The New York Times' Snow Fall in December 2012 [S1]
defining: A graphic pins in place while text scrolls past and updates it step by step [S1]
Scroll position, not a timer, triggers reveals, counting numbers and camera moves [S2]
Often built with GSAP or Three.js for data and product stories [S2]
Progress bars and numbered steps show how much of the story remains [S3]
fits: Data stories, annual reports, product launches, long-form features, nonprofit and museum stories
goes_wrong: Scrolljacking: the page fights the reader's scroll and feels broken on phones [S1]
accessibility: Never change scroll speed, keep text in reading order, and under reduced motion show every step as a plain static sequence.

name: Micrographics
plain: Tiny technical labels, grids, dots and lines used as decoration
origin: Labels, packaging and blueprints; named a 2026 layout trend by It's Nice That [S1], with dot grids and node lines named by Webflow [S2]
defining: Small type, symbols, timestamps, grids and diagram fragments used as page texture [S1]
Dot-grid backgrounds, node lines and wide open space, mostly for creative and generative tools [S2]
Mono or small-caps labels around 10 to 12px [inferred]
Thin rules and visible grids that signal specialist knowledge [S1]
fits: Canvas and generative tools, developer products, sportswear, hardware, technical brands
goes_wrong: Decorative micro text becomes unreadable noise or gets mistaken for real information
accessibility: Hide purely decorative labels from screen readers, keep real labels at 12px or more and 4.5:1, and keep dot grids faint behind text.

name: Sci-fi game UI
plain: Glowing cockpit screens with thin lines, gauges and data readouts
origin: Aviation head-up displays and film interface props [S2]; borrowed by web design as a 2025 trend [S1]
defining: Glowing edges, holographic elements and translucent layered panels [S1]
Electric blue, stark white and neon accents on deep blue-black [S1][S2]
Reticles, angular brackets and clipped corners; radius 0 to 4px [S2]
Condensed uppercase labels with monospaced numbers; scanning sweeps and data ticks [S2]
Differs from cyberpunk: borrows instrument panels, not neon city scenes
fits: Games, esports, simulations, AI agent and crypto launch pages, sci-fi campaigns
goes_wrong: Dense, dim telemetry nobody can read, worn like a costume over an ordinary site
accessibility: Translucent panels lose contrast: back text with a solid fill at 4.5:1, offer a reduced-transparency version, and stop scanning sweeps under reduced motion.
